blocks.text: When ionic compounds are dissolved in water, they are dissociated into ions, which are then surrounded by water molecules.

blocks.title: Hydration
blocks.text: “The process in which water molecules surround and interact with the solute ions is called hydration.”
The forces are created between water molecules and the ions which are called ion-dipole forces as shown in Figure 6.5. And as a result, all the ions in aqueous solution are said to be hydrated.

blocks.alt: An ionic lattice of yellow cations (+) and green anions (-). At the top a water molecule (red O with two white H) is pulled towards a cation with its O end, marked delta- on O and delta+ on H; at the bottom a water molecule is pulled towards an anion with its H ends, marked delta+ on H and delta- on O. Curved arrows lead from the lattice to a hydrated cation surrounded by six water molecules with O ends inward, and to a hydrated anion surrounded by six water molecules with H ends inward.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.5: Dissolution of an ionic compound through the process of hydration (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.5).

blocks.text: The energy of attraction due to an ion-dipole force is known as enthalpy of hydration, defined as follows:

blocks.title: Enthalpy of hydration
blocks.text: “The enthalpy change involved when one mole of a solute is dissolved in excess of water to make infinitely dilute solution under standard conditions.”
It is denoted by ΔHhyd. This energy is always released as it is formation of ion-dipole bond.

The heat of hydration depends on following factors:

We use a combined term for these two factors i.e., “charge density” defined as charge per unit area. If greater charge is present on smaller ion, the charge density is large and vice versa. And large value of charge density means that ions are strongly attracted by water molecules during the process of hydration, thereby increasing the hydration energy values.
